result.title: OMP Smart Approval

facts.text: The deliverable is a release-ready omp plugin package that semantically gates tool calls before execution and can be installed and exercised locally without publishing it.
Every in-scope call that omp would otherwise auto-approve, including calls in yolo and auto-approve sessions, passes through the full smart-approval gate before execution.

If omp would deny a call, the plugin skips judgment and preserves the denial. If omp would prompt, the judge performs one semantic pre-screen: a clear violation hard-blocks, while every other result is shown in a companion risk card and falls through to omp's single native prompt without a second approval dialog.
The judge evaluates every write-tier call, every exec-tier call, and every call whose arguments can transmit user-controlled data over the network, including URL reads and web searches.

Deterministic deny rules apply before ordinary scope filtering, so users can block local reads such as **/.env* or ~/.ssh/** without an LLM call. A successful local read, grep, or glob otherwise skips LLM judgment and updates provenance for later gated calls.
Every unknown custom or MCP tool is in scope for normal smart judgment unless the plugin can prove that the call is a purely local read with no external transmission.

The versioned built-in risk taxonomy covers prompt-injection-derived action, intent mismatch, destructive or irreversible effect, wrong target or environment, secret or private-data exposure, unexpected external side effect, privilege or supply-chain escalation, remote execution, safety-control tampering, and a catch-all other policy violation; examples within each category are not exhaustive attack signatures.
The judge does not gate ordinary code quality, architecture, style, efficiency, or non-consequential implementation choices.
A valid explicit configuration is required before any in-scope call can run; missing or invalid configuration fails closed with exact setup instructions and never opens an automatic first-use wizard.
The judge uses a fast authenticated model from an explicit provider allowlist and prefers a different model family from the primary session when an authorized contrasting model is available.

Judgment uses omp's model registry and authentication, so users do not supply a standalone judge API key. Every decision receives a fresh, tool-less judge context and provider-session identity, and total judge setup time is included in the latency measurement.

Each judge receives a fresh copy of the current primary-session intent and provenance context, but no mutable messages, verdicts, or provider-session state from earlier judgments; concurrent judgments cannot interleave state.
Verdicts are never cached; every in-scope call that lacks a human-created exact allow rule receives a fresh judgment.

The judge receives recent direct user intent, the proposed tool and arguments as fenced data, the primary coding agent's stated rationale, and a bounded recent-action trace containing tool names, argument summaries, and provenance flags.

Recent untrusted tool-output bodies are not copied into the judge prompt by default; the judge receives source, trust, timing, and action provenance instead, limiting prompt-injection exposure, cross-provider data sharing, tokens, and latency.

Before judge requests and persistent audit, the plugin reuses omp's secret machinery: secret-like environment values, user and project secrets.yml entries, and built-in credential-token patterns become deterministic typed placeholders; broader confidential business data remains governed by natural-language policy and semantic judgment.

If a tool argument field such as write content, an edit patch, shell heredoc, eval or browser code, or an MCP payload exceeds its configurable per-tool size threshold, that call cannot be silently allowed from a sample: it requires human escalation, while deterministic scanners inspect the complete value and report security findings.

The judge returns a validated structured verdict of allow, escalate, or block with risk classes, a concise rationale, and an optional policy-rule suggestion; malformed output is a judge failure, not an allow.
The judge may hard-block without prompting only for a clear safety or policy violation; legitimate-but-consequential and uncertain calls escalate to the human.

The default end-to-end judge target, including local judge setup, is five seconds with a ten-second per-attempt timeout and one retry for transient provider or transport failures; target, timeout, retry, and per-tool size settings are easy to configure.

For an omp-auto-approved call, judge timeout, provider error, malformed verdict, missing model, or internal error escalates to a human when possible and otherwise blocks. For a call omp already requires a human to approve, judge failure is shown prominently and only omp's native prompt can authorize execution.
An escalation allows execution only after an exact per-call nonce response from a real human interaction; default-returning, cancelled, dismissed, timed-out, or unsupported UI paths block.
An interactive escalation shows the literal pending tool call and arguments, source agent, judge rationale, risk classes, and matching policy before the human decides.

A headless subagent directly forwards a frozen escalation to extension code attached to the interactive main-session approval UI; the main agent model is not an intermediary, and approval is single-use, nonce-protected, time-limited, and bound to the exact call, repository, working directory, and policy version.

Before a subagent waits, it checks synchronously for a live main-session approval-UI handler. No handler causes an immediate visible and actionable block; an unanswered request blocks after a configurable timeout, and status remains visible by subagent ID and audit ID.
If the main session is also headless or cannot provide a trustworthy interaction channel, subagent escalation blocks rather than degrading to allow.

Every hard block, including a subagent block, is visible in the main UI and persistent audit with the fully qualified agent and parent IDs, tool-call and audit IDs, provenance sources, risk classes, rationale, timestamp, retry count, and current state; the blocked model also receives an actionable reason.

After three blocked attempts with the same deterministic retry-family key—source agent, tool, normalized operation, resolved target or destination, and risk class—the next attempt stops silent retrying and escalates the sequence to a human; without a human channel it remains blocked and tells the agent to stop retrying.

A human can deliberately override one blocked call by audit ID and typed per-call challenge; the resulting grant is exact-call-bound, single-use, short-lived, and invalidated by any argument or context change.

A human can persist an exact allow after a second confirmation; it defaults to project scope, includes repository and working-directory identity plus policy hash, requires explicit opt-in for user-wide scope, and remains listable and revocable.
A human-only session bypass requires typed confirmation, applies only to the current session, displays a persistent unguarded warning, and is recorded in the audit; the model cannot activate it.

Policy resolution is ordered: deterministic deny rules block first; narrow exact allow rules may skip the judge; broad allow patterns never skip judgment and only inform its posture; all remaining calls use the LLM judge.

Only a fully specified canonical allow with no wildcard, regex, capture, or omitted argument may skip judgment. An allow containing even one wildcard remains an allow-pattern hint and still receives LLM judgment.

Natural-language policy is discovered from user and project SMART_APPROVE.md files from broadest to most specific and is presented to the judge as authoritative policy, not untrusted transcript content.

Sensitivity has a balanced fallback plus per-tool or operation, per-risk-category, and rule-specific overrides. Risk-specific policy can remain strict even for a permissive tool, the narrowest applicable setting wins, and no sensitivity setting overrides deterministic denies or permits a missing verdict.

The judge may recommend an exact allow with no pattern operators, or an exact or patterned deny. Any allow containing even one wildcard is prohibited as a judge suggestion. Every suggestion is non-binding, previewed as a rule change, and applied only after explicit human confirmation.
The plugin's own configuration, policy files, and other active omp safety-policy files are protected from write and edit calls by the default deny floor unless the human explicitly overrides them.

Configuration exposes authorized providers and model preference, fallback and per-tool or per-risk sensitivity, tool and network scope overrides, per-tool argument-size thresholds, judge timeout and retry settings, escalation timeout, deterministic rules, and audit behavior.
The plugin provides commands to inspect status, run setup, list and revoke rules, review and override a block, and deliberately enter or leave session-only unguarded mode.

Every judgment persists compact redacted metadata: call ID and hash, source agent, tool, verdict, risk classes, concise rationale, matched rule, judge model, latency, and later override history; raw arguments, user messages, and secret values are not duplicated into the audit.

Deterministic automated tests cover tool scoping, policy precedence, model selection, context isolation, redaction, oversized arguments, structured verdict handling, every fail-closed path, secure UI defaults, subagent brokering, nonce and TTL behavior, loop breaking, overrides, bypass state, and audit redaction.

An opt-in live evaluation command runs a versioned benign, prompt-injection, exfiltration, destructive-action, wrong-target, and safety-tampering corpus against a configured real judge and reports false allows, false blocks, escalations, latency, session-construction overhead, token use, and cost by model and sensitivity.
Ordinary CI runs deterministic tests without provider credentials or paid model calls; live evaluations are opt-in and produce machine-readable reports that can support a future release gate.

The package includes installation and configuration documentation plus example deterministic and natural-language policies, and a smoke check proves that omp loads it and enforces one allowed, one escalated, and one blocked scenario locally.
